nameStory: The name "lespedeza" honors Vicente Manuel de Céspedes, an 18th-century Spanish governor of East Florida who supported botanical exploration. The species name "tomentosa" comes from the Latin word for "downy" or "woolly," referring to the soft, fuzzy hairs that cover this plant's stems and leaves like a cozy blanket.
description: Downy lespedeza is a medium-sized perennial wildflower that grows 1-3 feet tall in loose, open clusters. This native member of the legume family (the same plant family as peas and beans) has a distinctly fuzzy appearance due to soft hairs covering its stems and three-part leaves. In late summer, it produces small purple to pink pea-like flowers arranged in short, dense clusters. The whole plant has a soft, silvery-green appearance that makes it stand out in sunny meadows and woodland edges.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-part leaves (called trifoliate) with oval leaflets that feel distinctly soft and fuzzy to the touch, covered in dense, silky hairs that give them a grayish-green color

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small purple to pink pea-shaped flowers clustered in short, dense spikes at the ends of branches, blooming from July through September

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright perennial herb growing 1-3 feet tall with multiple stems that feel soft and downy when rubbed between your fingers

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, flattened seed pods that are also covered in soft hairs and contain a single seed, typical of the legume family

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Densely covered in soft, woolly hairs that give the entire plant a silvery, downy appearance, especially noticeable when backlit by sunlight

habitat: Downy lespedeza prefers dry, sandy soils in open areas like prairies, old fields, and woodland edges throughout New England, though it's quite rare in our region. You're most likely to find it in sunny spots with well-drained soil, often growing alongside other native wildflowers like goldenrod and asters. It thrives in areas that aren't too rich in nutrients, making it well-suited to poor, sandy soils that many other plants can't tolerate.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as fuzzy, three-part leaves on soft stems. The distinctive downy texture is already apparent on young foliage.
seasonality.summer: Purple to pink pea-shaped flowers bloom in dense clusters from July through August. The silvery, fuzzy foliage is at its most prominent.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and small, hairy seed pods develop. Leaves may turn yellowish before dying back, and seeds disperse in late fall.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving only roots alive underground. Dried stems and seed pods may persist into early winter.

funFact: Despite being a native wildflower, downy lespedeza is so rare in New England that it's been documented at only one location in the entire region, making it one of our most elusive botanical treasures!
confusionNotes: The soft, fuzzy three-part leaves make downy lespedeza fairly distinctive among New England's bush clovers. Other lespedezas in the region have much less fuzzy or nearly smooth leaves. Remember: if it feels like petting a rabbit when you touch the leaves, you've likely found downy lespedeza.
contextualKnowledge: The extreme rarity of downy lespedeza in New England likely reflects the northern edge of its natural range, as it's more common in the southeastern United States. Climate change may be affecting its ability to persist in our region.
compareHints: Downy lespedeza stands out from other bush clovers in New England primarily by its extremely fuzzy, silvery appearance. Round-headed bush clover has smooth or only slightly hairy leaves, while hairy lespedeza lives up to its name but still isn't as densely woolly as downy lespedeza. The dense, soft hairs covering every part of the plant make downy lespedeza unmistakable once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Round-headed bush clover stands out from its Lespedeza relatives by its distinctly round, compact flower heads - most other bush clovers have loose, elongated flower clusters or flowers scattered along the stems.
Among New England's bush clovers, hairy lespedeza stands out for its distinctly fuzzy, velvety texture covering the entire plant.
Among its bush clover relatives, violet bush clover stands out with its smooth (not hairy) stems and leaves, and its loose flower arrangement rather than dense round clusters.
Among New England's bush clovers, Chinese bushclover stands out for its silvery, densely hairy appearance and aggressive colonial growth habit.
Among New England's bush clovers, slender bush clover stands out for its delicate, wispy appearance with thin stems and small flower clusters.

Among its bush-clover relatives, tall bush-clover stands out with its reliably erect stems - round-headed bush clover has similar upright growth but denser, more rounded flower clusters, while violet bush clover and trailing lespedeza have more sprawling or leaning growth habits.
Among the many Lespedeza species, shrub lespedeza is unique in New England for its tall, shrubby growth habit - most other bush clovers in our region are low-growing or trailing plants.
Unlike its upright relatives like round-headed bush clover or hairy lespedeza that can reach several feet tall, trailing lespedeza never gets off the ground.
Among its bush clover relatives, narrow-leaved bush clover stands out for its distinctly slender leaflets and preference for wet soils.
Among the bush clovers in New England, violet bush clover stands out for its distinctly purple-violet flowers - most of its relatives have white, cream, or very pale pink blooms.
Among the lespedezas, Thunberg's is unique for its dramatic weeping form - most other bush clovers in New England grow upright or spreading but not with these long, graceful drooping branches.
While most of its lespedeza relatives like round-headed bush clover and violet bush clover grow upright in bushy clumps, creeping lespedeza is the ground-hugger of the family.
